content: 1. Contact investigation is a structured approach aimed at identifying undiagnosed tuberculosis (TB) cases among individuals who have been in contact with an index case. In certain contexts, this process also involves testing for latent TB infection (LTBI) to identify candidates for preventive treatment. The investigation includes steps such as identifying and prioritizing contacts, followed by clinical evaluation. 2. A high-TB-incidence country is defined as one with a World Health Organization (WHO)-estimated TB incidence rate of 100 or more cases per 100,000 population. 3. A household contact refers to an individual who has shared the same enclosed living space with the index case for at least one night or for frequent or extended daytime periods within the three months preceding the initiation of the index case's current TB treatment. 4. The index case (or index patient) of TB is the first identified case of new or recurrent TB in a person of any age within a specific household or comparable setting where others may have been exposed. The index case serves as the focal point for contact investigation but is not necessarily the source of the infection. 5. An infant is defined as a child under one year of age. 6. Latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) is a condition characterized by a persistent immune response to stimulation by Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without any clinical evidence of active TB disease. There is no definitive test available for directly identifying Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection in humans. 7. A low-TB-incidence country is one with a WHO-estimated TB incidence rate of fewer than 100 cases per 100,000 population. 8. Preventive treatment refers to the administration of therapy to individuals at risk of developing TB disease to reduce that risk. This is also known as LTBI treatment or preventive therapy. 9. Tuberculosis (TB) refers to the disease state caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In this context, it is often referred to as active TB or TB disease to distinguish it from LTBI. 10. LTBI is defined as a state of persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without clinical evidence of active TB. There is no gold standard test for LTBI. WHO guidelines on LTBI consider factors such as the likelihood of progression to active TB in specific risk groups, TB epidemiology and burden, resource availability, and potential public health impact. 11. WHO has consolidated guidelines for LTBI management in response to requests from member states. These guidelines provide comprehensive recommendations for programmatic management of LTBI and serve as a basis for national guidelines. They replace previous WHO policy documents on LTBI management in people living with HIV, household contacts of TB patients, and other at-risk groups. 12. The updated guidelines were developed following WHO's recommended processes, including seven systematic reviews to update and create new recommendations. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) evaluated evidence quality, benefits and harms, values and preferences, equity, costs, acceptability, and feasibility to formulate recommendations and determine their strength. 13. Recommendations are organized according to the cascade of care for LTBI management: identifying at-risk populations, ruling out active TB, testing for LTBI, providing treatment, monitoring adverse events, ensuring adherence and treatment completion, and monitoring and evaluation. 14. Recommendations are categorized as existing (previously approved and still valid), updated (previously approved but revised based on new evidence), and new. There are 10 existing, 7 updated, and 7 new recommendations. 15. The GDG reviewed evidence on LTBI prevalence, risk of progression to active TB, and active TB incidence in specific risk groups compared to the general population. The guiding principle was that individual benefit outweighs risk in recommendations for LTBI testing and treatment. 16. Systematic testing and treatment of LTBI are strongly recommended for people living with HIV and for infants and children under five years of age who are household contacts of pulmonary TB patients, regardless of TB epidemiology. 17. HIV-negative groups at clinical risk, such as patients initiating anti-TNF treatment, receiving dialysis, preparing for organ or hematological transplantation, or with silicosis, should also undergo LTBI testing and treatment due to their increased risk of progression to active TB. 18. Adults, adolescents, children, and infants living with HIV should receive TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of their degree of immunosuppression, ART status, previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. 19. Infants under 12 months living with HIV who are in contact with a TB case and have no active TB disease should receive six months of isoniazid preventive treatment (IPT). 20. Children aged 12 months or older living with HIV in high-TB-prevalence settings should be offered six months of IPT as part of comprehensive HIV prevention and care if they are unlikely to have TB disease and have no contact with a TB case. 21. All children living with HIV who have completed TB treatment may receive an additional six months of isoniazid. 22. HIV-negative children under five years who are household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB patients and have no active TB should receive TB preventive treatment. 23. In low-TB-incidence countries, systematic testing and treatment for LTBI are recommended for household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB patients. 24. In high-TB-incidence countries, children aged five years or older, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB patients and have no active TB may be given TB preventive treatment. 25. Patients initiating anti-TNF treatment, receiving dialysis, preparing for organ or hematological transplantation, or with silicosis should be systematically tested and treated for LTBI. 26. In low-TB-incidence countries, systematic LTBI testing and treatment may be considered for prisoners, health workers, immigrants from high-TB-burden countries, homeless people, and people who use illicit drugs. 27. Systematic LTBI testing is not recommended for people with diabetes, harmful alcohol use, tobacco smokers, or underweight individuals unless they are included in the above recommendations. 28. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered preventive treatment. 29. Chest radiography may be offered to people living with HIV on ART, and preventive treatment should be given to those with no abnormal radiographic findings. 30. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who report symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats should be evaluated for TB and other diseases causing these symptoms. 31. Infants and children living with HIV with poor weight gain, fever, cough, or a history of contact with a TB case should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If no TB is found, they should be offered preventive treatment. 32. The absence of TB symptoms and abnormal chest radiographic findings may be used to rule out active TB in HIV-negative household contacts aged five years or older and other at-risk groups before preventive treatment. 33. Either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) can be used to test for LTBI. 34. People living with HIV who test positive for LTBI benefit more from preventive treatment than those who test negative. LTBI testing can be used, where feasible, to identify such individuals. 35. LTBI testing is not required to initiate preventive treatment in people living with HIV or child household contacts under five years of age. 36. Isoniazid monotherapy for six months is recommended for LTBI treatment in both adults and children in highand low-TB-incidence countries. 37. Rifampicin plus isoniazid daily for three months is an alternative to six months of isoniazid monotherapy for children and adolescents under 15 years in high-TB-incidence countries. 38. Rifapentine and isoniazid weekly for three months may be offered as an alternative to six months of isoniazid monotherapy for both adults and children in high-TB-incidence countries. 39. In low-TB-incidence countries, alternative LTBI treatment options include nine months of isoniazid, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, three to four months of isoniazid plus rifampicin, or three to four months of rifampicin alone. 40. In high-TB-incidence settings, adults and adolescents living with HIV with a positive or unknown TST and no active TB should receive at least 36 months of IPT, regardless of ART status, immunosuppression, previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. 41. Preventive treatment may be considered for selected high-risk household contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant TB based on individualized risk assessment and sound clinical justification. 42. Adverse events during preventive treatment must be minimized. Individuals receiving LTBI treatment should be monitored regularly, with monthly visits to healthcare providers. Patients should be educated about the disease, the rationale for treatment, and the importance of completing it. 43. Patients should be encouraged to contact healthcare providers if they develop symptoms such as anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, fatigue, dark urine, pale stools, or jaundice. If a healthcare provider is unavailable, treatment should be stopped immediately. 44. Adherence to and completion of preventive treatment are critical for clinical benefit and program success. Interventions should be tailored to the specific needs of risk groups and local contexts to ensure adherence and treatment completion. 45. National programs should develop plans for the programmatic management of LTBI, prioritizing high-risk groups.
